Question B-006-005-004.

Why the correct answer is right: An open or short circuit is an extreme impedance error. Either condition reflects most of the RF energy, so the SWR can become very high.

Why the distractors are wrong:
- sourceIndex 1: "Grounding the shield of the coaxial cable at the building entrance": Bonding the coax shield at the building entrance is a normal grounding and lightning-safety practice; by itself it does not create an antenna-feed impedance mismatch.
- sourceIndex 2: "Using a very long transmission line": A very long lossy line often hides a mismatch by attenuating the reflected wave on its return trip, so it can make the station-end SWR look lower rather than higher.
- sourceIndex 3: "Replacing RG-213 coaxial cable with RG-58": RG-58 and RG-213 are both commonly 50-ohm coax types; replacing RG-213 with RG-58 may increase loss and power-heating concerns, but the cable swap alone is not a high-SWR cause.
